title: Docker Complete Handbook
summary: A start-to-production study series on Docker: architecture and internals, images and containers, Dockerfile build optimization, storage, networking, Compose, registries, security, debugging, and orchestration, closing with interview questions and a cheatsheet.

chapters.title: Docker
points: Docker packages an app plus its dependencies into an image that runs as an isolated container on any host with a container runtime
Containers share the host kernel, so they start in milliseconds and use far less memory than VMs
Series map: architecture, images, Dockerfile, storage, networking, Compose, registries, security, debugging, production
Core vocabulary: image, container, layer, registry, Dockerfile, volume, network
Docker Engine, Docker Desktop and Docker CLI are different things: Desktop bundles Engine in a Linux VM on macOS and Windows
Typical workflow: write Dockerfile, build image, push to registry, pull and run on any host
Why it matters: reproducible environments, 'works on my machine' disappears, fast CI and deploys

chapters.title: Docker Architecture and Internals
points: Client-server model: the docker CLI talks to the dockerd daemon over a REST API on /var/run/docker.sock
dockerd delegates container lifecycle to containerd, which calls runc through a containerd-shim
runc is the OCI runtime that creates the container using kernel primitives, then exits
Namespaces isolate what a process sees: pid, net, mnt, uts, ipc, user
cgroups limit and account for resources: CPU, memory, block IO, pids
Union filesystems (overlay2) stack read-only image layers with one writable container layer
Copy-on-write: a file is copied up to the writable layer only when a container modifies it
OCI specs standardize image format and runtime, so images work across Docker, Podman and containerd
Container vs VM: a container is an isolated process on a shared kernel, a VM runs its own guest kernel on a hypervisor
Access to docker.sock is effectively root on the host, so never expose it casually

chapters.title: Images and Containers
points: An image is an immutable stack of read-only layers plus a config JSON; a container is a running instance of it
Image names: registry/namespace/repo:tag, and a digest like @sha256:... pins exact content
Tags are mutable pointers; digests are immutable
Container lifecycle states: created, running, paused, exited, dead; commands docker create, start, stop, kill, rm
docker run = pull if missing + create + start; flags -d, -it, --rm, --name, -p, -e
docker stop sends SIGTERM then SIGKILL after 10s grace; docker kill sends SIGKILL immediately
docker exec runs an extra process in a running container; docker attach connects to PID 1 streams
docker ps -a lists stopped containers too; docker images and docker image prune manage local images
Restart policies: no, on-failure[:max], always, unless-stopped
Mistake: depending on :latest, which makes builds non-reproducible
Mistake: storing data in the container writable layer, which is lost on docker rm
Resource limits: --memory, --cpus; exceeding memory gets the process OOM-killed with exit code 137

chapters.title: Dockerfile Essentials and Build Optimization
points: Core instructions: FROM, RUN, COPY, ADD, WORKDIR, ENV, ARG, EXPOSE, USER, CMD, ENTRYPOINT
Each RUN, COPY and ADD creates a layer; chain related commands with && to keep layers few
Layer cache: a changed instruction invalidates the cache for every instruction after it
Order for caching: copy dependency manifests first, install, then copy source
COPY vs ADD: prefer COPY; ADD also extracts tars and fetches URLs, which surprises people
CMD vs ENTRYPOINT: ENTRYPOINT is the fixed executable, CMD supplies default arguments that run overrides
Exec form ["node","app.js"] receives signals as PID 1; shell form wraps in /bin/sh -c and swallows SIGTERM
Multi-stage builds: FROM node AS build, then COPY --from=build into a slim final stage to drop toolchains
Small bases: alpine, distroless, slim, or scratch for static binaries; alpine uses musl, which can break glibc binaries
BuildKit features: parallel stages, --mount=type=cache, --mount=type=secret, and build secrets that never land in layers
A .dockerignore keeps node_modules, .git and secrets out of the build context
Mistake: apt-get update in its own RUN gets cached stale; combine it with install and clean /var/lib/apt/lists

chapters.title: Volumes and Storage
points: Container writable layer is ephemeral and slower than a volume because of copy-on-write
Three mount types: named volume, bind mount, tmpfs
Named volumes are managed by Docker under /var/lib/docker/volumes and are the preferred way to persist data
Bind mounts map a host path into the container; great for dev hot reload, but depend on host layout and permissions
tmpfs mounts live in memory only and vanish on stop; good for secrets and scratch data
-v src:dst vs --mount type=...,src=...,dst=...: --mount is explicit and errors on a missing source, while -v silently creates a directory
Anonymous volumes get random names and pile up; docker volume prune removes unused ones
Mount flags: :ro for read-only; a volume is initialized with the image content at that path on first use
docker volume create, ls, inspect, rm; --volumes-from shares volumes between containers
Back up a volume by running a throwaway container that tars the mount to a bind mount
Volume drivers (NFS, cloud block storage) allow shared or remote storage
Mistake: bind mount over a directory hides the image contents there, such as node_modules

chapters.title: Docker Networking
points: Default drivers: bridge, host, none, overlay, macvlan
Default bridge network docker0 gives containers NAT access out, but no name resolution between them
User-defined bridge networks add automatic DNS by container name via the embedded resolver at 127.0.0.11
Port publishing -p host:container installs iptables DNAT rules; EXPOSE is only documentation
Host driver shares the host network stack: no isolation, no port mapping, best raw performance on Linux
none gives only loopback; overlay spans multiple hosts for Swarm; macvlan gives containers their own MAC address on the LAN
Container-to-container: use the service name on a shared network, never the container IP
Bind -p 127.0.0.1:8080:80 to avoid exposing a port on all interfaces
docker network create, connect, disconnect, inspect; a container can join multiple networks
Reach the host from a container with host.docker.internal on Desktop, or --add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway on Linux
Mistake: app listens on 127.0.0.1 inside the container, so published ports never connect; bind to 0.0.0.0
Mistake: published ports bypass ufw/firewalld rules because Docker edits iptables directly

chapters.title: Docker Compose
points: Compose defines a multi-container app in one compose.yaml and runs it with docker compose up
Top-level keys: services, networks, volumes, configs, secrets
Service fields: image, build, ports, environment, env_file, volumes, depends_on, command, restart
Compose creates a default project network, so services reach each other by service name
depends_on controls start order only; use condition: service_healthy with a healthcheck to wait for readiness
healthcheck: test, interval, timeout, retries, start_period
Variable substitution ${VAR:-default} and .env file; env_file loads vars into the container
Profiles start optional services selectively, such as debug tools or seed jobs
Override files: compose.override.yaml merges automatically, or pass -f to layer prod over base
Commands: up -d, down (-v also removes volumes), logs -f, ps, exec, build, config to render the final file
docker compose watch syncs or rebuilds on file change for fast dev loops
Compose v2 is the docker compose plugin; the old docker-compose v1 binary is retired
Mistake: down -v deletes named volumes and your database data

chapters.title: Registries and Image Distribution
points: A registry stores and serves images by repo and tag: Docker Hub, GHCR, ECR, GCR/Artifact Registry, ACR, self-hosted Harbor or registry:2
Push flow: docker login, docker tag, docker push; only layers missing remotely are uploaded
Layers are content-addressed by sha256, so identical layers are stored and pulled once
A manifest lists layer digests and config; a manifest list or index selects the image per architecture
Multi-arch builds with docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 --push
Tagging strategy: immutable version tags, git SHA tags, and a moving latest only for convenience
Pin deployments by digest for exact reproducibility
Docker Hub applies pull rate limits to anonymous users; use authenticated pulls or a pull-through cache mirror
Private registries need credentials: docker login stores them in config.json, preferably through a credential helper
Image retention and garbage collection policies keep registry cost under control
Mistake: pushing images with baked-in secrets, because every layer is readable by anyone who can pull

chapters.title: Docker Security
points: The container boundary is weaker than a VM, so defence in depth is needed
Run as non-root with USER; root in a container is root on the host if it escapes
Drop capabilities with --cap-drop=ALL and add back only what is needed
--read-only root filesystem plus tmpfs for writable paths
--security-opt no-new-privileges blocks setuid privilege escalation
Default seccomp profile blocks about 44 risky syscalls; AppArmor or SELinux add mandatory access control
Never use --privileged or mount /var/run/docker.sock into app containers
Rootless mode and user namespace remapping (userns-remap) map container root to an unprivileged host UID
Scan images for CVEs with Docker Scout, Trivy or Grype in CI
Use minimal or distroless bases, pinned digests and Docker Content Trust or cosign signatures
Secrets: use BuildKit secret mounts or runtime secrets, not ENV or ARG, because both are visible in docker history and inspect
Mistake: running the daemon API over unauthenticated TCP 2375, which gives remote root

chapters.title: Debugging and Troubleshooting
points: Check state first: docker ps -a, then docker inspect for exit code, OOMKilled flag, mounts and network
docker logs -f --tail 100 --since 10m reads the stdout and stderr streams; the logging driver decides storage
Exit codes: 0 clean, 1 app error, 125 daemon error, 126 not executable, 127 command not found, 137 SIGKILL or OOM, 143 SIGTERM
docker exec -it c sh to look inside; for images without a shell use docker debug or a sidecar sharing namespaces
docker stats and docker top show live CPU, memory and processes
docker events streams daemon activity such as die, oom and health_status
Crash loop: restart policy hides the failure, so read logs of the previous attempt and run the image with the entrypoint overridden to sh
Cannot connect: verify the app binds 0.0.0.0, the port is published, containers share a network, DNS resolves with nslookup
Disk full: docker system df shows usage; docker system prune and builder prune reclaim space
Build failures: docker build --progress=plain --no-cache reveals the failing step
Permission denied on volumes: UID mismatch between container user and host files
Mistake: debugging by editing a running container, which is lost on recreate; fix the Dockerfile instead

chapters.title: Production and Orchestration
points: Production containers should be stateless, disposable and configured through environment
Healthchecks and restart policies provide basic self-healing on a single host
Set memory and CPU limits and reservations so one container cannot starve a host
Handle SIGTERM for graceful shutdown and set stop_grace_period; use an init process (--init, tini) to reap zombies
Log to stdout and ship with a logging driver (json-file with max-size and max-file, or fluentd, gelf) to avoid disks filling
Docker Swarm: built-in orchestration with services, replicas, overlay networks, secrets and rolling updates
Kubernetes is the industry standard orchestrator: pods, deployments, services, autoscaling, and a far larger ecosystem than Swarm
Orchestrators add scheduling, service discovery, rolling and rollback deploys, and auto-scaling across many hosts
Choose by scale: Compose for one host, Swarm for simple clusters, Kubernetes or a managed service (ECS, Cloud Run) for serious scale
CI/CD pipeline: build, test, scan, push by SHA, deploy by digest, with a rollback to the previous digest
Mistake: running one big container with many processes instead of one process per container
Mistake: no log rotation, so json-file logs fill the disk

chapters.title: Docker Interview Questions and Cheatsheet
points: Q: Image vs container? An image is the read-only template, a container is a running instance with a writable layer
Q: CMD vs ENTRYPOINT, and exec vs shell form
Q: COPY vs ADD, and why multi-stage builds shrink images
Q: Volume vs bind mount vs tmpfs, and when to use each
Q: Why can't containers on the default bridge resolve each other by name?
Q: depends_on vs healthcheck, and how to make a service wait for its database
Q: How do namespaces and cgroups make a container?
Q: Container vs VM trade-offs
Cheat: docker build -t app . ; docker run -d --name app -p 8080:80 app ; docker logs -f app ; docker exec -it app sh
Cheat: docker compose up -d --build ; docker compose down ; docker system prune -af
Best practices: small pinned base, non-root user, one process per container, .dockerignore, scan images, never bake secrets
